connections.feedback: Yes. A claim from one classmate is a starting point, not proof. Asking where it came from, then finding a second source, is a quick way to find out. If two independent places agree, you can use it; if not, you have learned something too.
Being well known is not the same as being true. Many popular claims were repeated without ever being checked. A famous claim still needs a check before it goes on a poster.

This is honest about how sure you are, which is better than stating it as fact. The cost is that a poster is read as information, and "some people say" can still spread a claim nobody checked. Checking first would cost only a few minutes.
connections.notes: Hedging wording is a real trade-off: it is more honest than flat fact, but still publishes an unchecked claim.

connections.feedback: The claim came second-hand, but that is a reason to check it, not to throw it out. It could be true. Dropping it unchecked skips the step that would tell you.

connections.feedback: Yes. You get two checks: where the claim started, and whether an independent record agrees. Both are cheap here and they answer different worries, one about the origin and one about whether the claim holds up.
A claim being widely repeated tells you it spreads easily, not that it is accurate. Repetition can come from one original mistake copied many times.
Hedging is more honest than flat fact, but it still hands the audience a claim you did not check. It is a reasonable choice only if no time is left and the claim is low stakes.
connections.notes: Reasonable under time pressure; the hidden cost is that hedged claims are still remembered as facts.

connections.feedback: Second-hand does not mean false. The better move is to find out where it came from. Dropping it quietly means you never learn whether it was right.

connections.feedback: Yes. The deadline and the doubt both matter. Sending the report with the figure clearly marked as unchecked keeps the work moving and makes sure the reader is not misled. You can follow up with the teammate as soon as they return.

Waiting avoids passing on a possible error, which is a real strength. The cost is that your manager gets nothing at the deadline, and may have been able to use the rest. Whether this is better depends on how damaging a wrong figure would be.
connections.notes: Safe on accuracy, expensive on timing. Defensible if the figure drives a decision.

connections.feedback: The figure looked wrong to you and you sent it with no warning. If it is wrong, the reader trusts it because it looks finished. Your doubt was information, and the report hid it.

Asking and cross-checking is the right habit in general. Here the teammate is away and the clock is short, so this option may not be possible in time. It becomes strong again if you can reach someone quickly.
connections.notes: Good practice that may not fit the time available.

connections.feedback: Yes. The three weeks are gone whichever way you go, so they should not decide the choice. What matters is what each path costs and delivers from today. This keeps the decision about the future.
This is the sunk-cost trap: treating time already spent as a reason to continue. The work would be "wasted" either way if the plan cannot meet its goal. Continuing only adds more cost.
Momentum and team morale are real and forward-looking, so they belong in the comparison. The risk is that they become a reason to ignore a flaw that means the goal is missed.
connections.notes: Morale is a legitimate cost of restarting; it should be weighed, not used to end the discussion.

connections.feedback: A newer idea is not better because it is newer. Switching because the old plan feels tired replaces one bias with another. Compare the two on what they deliver.

This jumps from "go together" to "one causes the other". If motivation drives both, forcing visits may change little. The plan could cost time and goodwill and still not move grades.
A link between two things is a clue, even when it is not proof of cause. Ignoring it throws away something worth investigating.

A small trial is a good way to test cause, and it is much better than acting on the pattern alone. It costs time and needs a fair comparison, so it is the next step after you ask why the groups differ.
connections.notes: A good second step. As a first response it skips thinking about other explanations.

Yes. Damage is rare to begin with (about 1 in 200), and flags are common (about 1 in 20). So at most about 1 in 10 flagged boxes can be damaged, which means most are fine. Staying calm reflects the numbers.
The check is a weak signal and most flagged boxes are fine. Refusing sends back goods that are probably good and upsets the customer without any look at the box.
The check does give many false alarms, so skepticism is reasonable. But a flag still shifts the odds, and ignoring it entirely would miss the few boxes that really are damaged.
connections.notes: Skeptical of the test, yet discards a signal that is cheap to follow up with a quick look.

Reporting is defensible, especially if rules require it or you suspect it is deliberate. The cost is that you skip a chance to let an honest mistake be corrected, and the coworker may feel accused.

connections.feedback: Yes. AI assistants can produce quotes, titles and authors that sound right but do not exist. A confident tone is not evidence. Find the passage in the book or a reliable source before using it.
Sounding sure is not a sign of being right. Assistants can invent details that look real. Using the quote unchecked risks putting a made-up source in your work.
Keeping the quote private until it is checked is safe and sensible. The risk is that unchecked drafts get copied forward and forgotten, so a reminder to verify matters.
connections.notes: Defensible as a holding step; the hidden cost is the check being forgotten.

connections.feedback: One bad quote is a reason to check this kind of output, not to stop using the tool for everything. Throwing the tool away is an overreaction.
